name: Greenock
title: Greenock Ship Gauging | UTM at Garvel Dock and Ocean Terminal
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement at Greenock for ferries, container feeders and cruise ships: hull gauging in the Garvel dry dock, tanks and piping afloat.
h1: Hull, Tank and Piping Thickness Measurement for Ships at Greenock
intro: Greenock stands where the River Clyde opens into its firth, and its waterfront combines Ocean Terminal's container and cruise berths with ship repair at the Garvel dry dock. West-coast ferries, newbuilds from the Port Glasgow yard and feeder container ships all pass through, and a docking or a lay-by berth on the Clyde gives the time thickness gauging needs. We bring technicians from India to the ship, whether she is in the dock, alongside or at anchor off the town.

highlights.p: Dales Marine Services runs the Garvel dry dock in Greenock, used by ferries and other vessels for refits and class dockings. With the hull dry, bottom shell, sea chests and the stern area can be gauged and the steel list agreed before the dock is flooded again.

highlights.h: Feeder and cruise calls at Ocean Terminal
highlights.p: Greenock Ocean Terminal handles container feeders and is the Clyde's main cruise berth. Feeder ships turn round quickly, so their gauging is targeted and planned well ahead, while cruise ships offer a few hours alongside for piping and deck work.

highlights.h: Lay-by berths and anchorages on the Clyde
highlights.p: Ships waiting for orders, a docking slot or a new owner can lie at the Clyde's lay-by berths or anchor off Greenock. Longer stays like these allow full tank programmes, owner's condition surveys and pre-purchase gauging without the pressure of a cargo schedule.

port.h: Greenock on the Firth of Clyde: terminal, repair yard and anchorage
p: The Clyde narrows above Greenock, and the town has long marked the point where seagoing ships give way to river traffic heading up to Glasgow. Below it, the Firth of Clyde opens south towards Arran and the North Channel, giving a sheltered approach from the Irish Sea that the Kintyre peninsula and the islands screen from the full Atlantic swell. The stretch of water off Greenock and Gourock, known as the Tail of the Bank, has long served as an anchorage for ships waiting to go upriver or out to sea. Peel Ports operates the port through Clydeport, providing pilotage and managing the terminals, docks and berths from Greenock up to Glasgow. Ships of moderate draught can therefore choose between a terminal berth, a repair dock, a lay-by quay and an anchorage within a short distance of one another.

Greenock Ocean Terminal is the main commercial berth on this part of the river, handling container feeder services that connect Scotland's west coast with larger hub ports, and doubling as the Clyde's principal cruise terminal, with a dedicated building for passengers. The region's ferry network is centred on the firth, with CalMac routes from Gourock, Wemyss Bay and Ardrossan crossing to Dunoon, Bute and Arran, and the ferries that serve them need regular dockings, some of which are taken on the Clyde. Shipbuilding continues upriver at Port Glasgow, where Ferguson Marine builds ferries, and at the naval yards in Glasgow itself. General cargo and bulk ships also work the river's other berths, so the mix of tonnage passing Greenock is wider than its own terminal suggests.

Ship repair on this stretch of the Clyde is concentrated at Greenock. The Garvel dry dock, operated by Dales Marine Services, takes ferries and other vessels for refits and dockings, including newbuilds before delivery: the Ferguson-built ferry Glen Rosa went into the dock in 2025. Upriver at Inchgreen, Peel Ports owns Scotland's largest drydock, which has been out of regular use for many years and has been the subject of plans to bring it back into service, most recently for ship decommissioning. Weather on the Clyde is wet and windy rather than icy, and the sheltered upper firth keeps most work possible all year, though strong westerlies can interrupt boat transfers to ships at anchor and slow outdoor work on deck.

facilities.h: Docks, berths and anchorages for gauging on the Clyde
p: For a renewal survey or a docking survey, the Garvel dry dock is the place at Greenock where a hull can be gauged out of the water. The team works to the yard's programme and the agreed TM plan with the class surveyor attending, starting on the bottom shell, sea chests and stern frame while staging and lighting are in place, then moving to tanks as they are gas-freed. Because the dock is sized for ferries and coastal and short-sea ships rather than large ocean-going tonnage, bigger vessels trading to the Clyde dock elsewhere, and a Greenock call before that docking is a good time to measure the steel the yard will need to renew.

Afloat, the options depend on the ship's business. Feeder container ships at Ocean Terminal turn round in hours, so their scope is limited to what can be done during cargo work: deck plating, hatch coamings, air pipes and engine-room piping. Cruise ships allow a similar window. Ships with time to spare, waiting for a docking slot, laid up, or changing hands, can lie at a lay-by berth such as James Watt Dock or anchor off Greenock, where the agent arranges boat transfers. Those longer stays suit complete ballast tank programmes and the condition surveys that buyers and owners rely on.
list: Garvel dry dock — bottom shell, sea chest, stern and tank gauging during refits and class dockings, worked to the yard programme.
Greenock Ocean Terminal — deck, hatch coaming and piping readings on container feeders and cruise ships during their time alongside.
James Watt Dock and other Clyde lay-by berths — full tank programmes on ships waiting for a docking slot, laid up or changing hands.
Anchorages off Greenock — targeted deck and tank gauging by boat transfer on ships awaiting orders or a berth upriver.
Ferry lay-over berths on the firth — sea-water piping, car-deck and void-space checks on ferries between sailings or out of season.

context.h: The Clyde's regulatory picture: MCA, recycling rules and ferries
p: Port state control on the Clyde is in the hands of the Maritime and Coastguard Agency, applying the Paris MoU inspection regime through UK law, and the feeder container ships and occasional bulk and general cargo ships calling here are its usual subjects. Greenock lies on the west coast, outside the North Sea emission control area that begins on the far side of Scotland. Feeders that continue to the east coast or the Continent switch fuel or rely on their scrubbers when they enter it, so their wash-water and fuel piping work under two regimes on a single rotation, which is worth remembering when the piping scope is drawn up.

Ship recycling is an unusual part of the picture here. The UK kept the EU Ship Recycling Regulation in its own law after Brexit, so UK-flagged ships must be recycled at approved facilities and carry an Inventory of Hazardous Materials, and ships of other flags calling at UK ports are expected to have one as well. With the Hong Kong Convention in force internationally since June 2025 and plans to use Inchgreen for decommissioning, owners of older tonnage on the Clyde increasingly need a clear record of their ship's condition. Ferries add a domestic dimension: UK passenger ships are surveyed by the MCA, and their operators plan steel and piping renewal around tight seasonal timetables.

jobs.h: Gauging work we see at Greenock
jobs.p: Greenock jobs fall into three kinds. Docking work at Garvel follows the yard's programme and the class survey, with readings feeding the steel renewal list while the ship is in the dock. Short calls at Ocean Terminal need a scope fixed in advance and tanks prepared by the crew. Longer stays at lay-by berths and anchorages, which come with sales, lay-ups and waits for a docking slot, allow the widest programmes. We plan each with the superintendent, the agent and, where the ship is docking, the yard, so that staging, gas-freeing and access are ready when the team arrives. Readings are reported against the ship's frames and strakes.
list: Renewal-survey gauging on a ferry in the Garvel dry dock, with substantial corrosion marked on the shell for the yard to renew before undocking.
Pre-docking steel estimate for a container feeder, gauged over successive calls at Ocean Terminal ahead of a docking elsewhere.
Pre-purchase hull and tank gauging on a ship laid up at a Clyde lay-by berth, scoped by the buyer's technical adviser.
Scrubber wash-water and overboard piping UT on a cruise ship during a summer call at Greenock.
Sea chest, sea-water piping and stern area checks on a workboat or offshore vessel during a short docking.

logistics: Glasgow Airport is the closest international airport, with Glasgow Prestwick and Edinburgh as alternatives, and trains and roads run from Glasgow along the south bank of the Clyde to Greenock. The technicians are mobilised from India and need UK visas, so early notice of a docking date or a ship's lay-by period helps. Dry dock access is arranged with Dales Marine Services, terminal passes through Peel Ports, and boat transfers to anchored ships are booked by the ship's agent.
vessels: Laid-up ships awaiting sale or recycling

faqs.q: Can you gauge a ship in the Garvel dry dock in Greenock?
faqs.a: Yes, for the owner or manager of a ship docking there. We follow the yard's programme and the TM plan agreed with the class surveyor, take shell and sea chest readings while the hull is dry, and move to tanks as they are certified gas-free. Areas of substantial or excessive corrosion are marked on the steel and passed to the yard straight away, so renewal can be ordered before undocking.

faqs.q: What can be gauged on a container feeder during a call at Ocean Terminal?
faqs.a: A feeder's call is short and cargo work dominates it, so the scope is targeted: deck plating, hatch covers and coamings, air pipes and engine-room piping, plus a ballast tank if the crew has emptied and ventilated it beforehand. Repeated calls on a regular rotation let a larger programme be completed in stages, which suits a pre-docking steel estimate.

faqs.q: Is the Inchgreen dry dock available for ship repair?
faqs.a: Inchgreen, owned by Peel Ports, has been out of regular use for many years, and recent plans for it have focused on ship decommissioning rather than repair. Owners planning a Clyde docking should check its status at the time; for most ships the working option at Greenock is the Garvel dry dock, and larger vessels dock at yards elsewhere in the UK or Europe.

faqs.q: Can a laid-up ship be surveyed at anchor off Greenock?
faqs.a: Yes, with boat transfers arranged by the agent and when the weather permits. A laid-up or waiting ship can have tanks emptied and ventilated over several days, so a full condition survey is realistic: shell, deck, ballast and cargo spaces, and piping. That record is what a buyer, an insurer or an owner reactivating the ship usually needs before committing to repairs.

faqs.q: How is gauging arranged on a west-coast ferry docking on the Clyde?
faqs.a: We work with the operator's superintendent and the yard from the docking specification. Ferries have tight seasonal timetables, so the plan sets out which car-deck, void-space, ballast tank and sea-water piping readings are needed and in what order, and the UK visa and travel arrangements are made against the docking date. Findings are shared daily so renewal can be agreed within the docking period.
